We can proceed in interpreting and using the model for prediction.

<!-- ======================================================================== -->
# Interpretation and Inference {#sec-interpretation}
<!-- ======================================================================== -->

## Model Equation

The final model includes 10 main predictors plus one interaction term between `study_hrs` and `sleep_qual`. The regression equation is:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\hat{y} = &\ \beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot \text{attend\_pct} + \beta_2 \cdot \text{study\_hrs} + \beta_3 \cdot \text{sleep\_hrs} \\
&+ \beta_4 \cdot \mathbb{1}_{\text{trav\_time = 15-30 Min}} + \beta_5 \cdot \mathbb{1}_{\text{trav\_time = 30-60 Min}} + \beta_6 \cdot \mathbb{1}_{\text{trav\_time > 60 Min}} \\
&+ \beta_7 \cdot \mathbb{1}_{\text{sleep\_qual = Average}} + \beta_8 \cdot \mathbb{1}_{\text{sleep\_qual = Good}} \\
&+ \sum_{k=1}^{5} \gamma_k \cdot \mathbb{1}_{\text{parent\_educ = level } k} \\
&+ \delta_1 \cdot \mathbb{1}_{\text{extra\_act = Yes}} + \delta_2 \cdot \mathbb{1}_{\text{web\_access = Yes}} + \delta_3 \cdot \mathbb{1}_{\text{school\_type = Private}} \\
&+ \sum_{m=1}^{5} \phi_m \cdot \mathbb{1}_{\text{study\_method = method } m} \\
&+ \lambda_1 \cdot (\text{study\_hrs} \times \mathbb{1}_{\text{sleep\_qual = Average}}) \\
&+ \lambda_2 \cdot (\text{study\_hrs} \times \mathbb{1}_{\text{sleep\_qual = Good}})
\end{aligned}
$$

where $\mathbb{1}_{\{\cdot\}}$ denotes indicator (dummy) variables.

## Reference Categories

For each categorical variable, one level is absorbed into the intercept as the **reference category**. All coefficients for that variable represent differences relative to this reference.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-references
#| tbl-cap: "Reference categories for categorical variables (absorbed in intercept)"

reference_table <- data.frame(
  Variable = c("school_type", "parent_educ", "sleep_qual", "trav_time", 
               "extra_act", "web_access", "study_method"),
  Reference = c("Public", "No Formal", "Poor", "<15 Min", "No", "No", "Online Videos"),
  Other_Levels = c("Private",
                   "High School, Graduate, Post Grad 1, Post Grad 2, PhD",
                   "Average, Good",
                   "15-30 Min, 30-60 Min, >60 Min",
                   "Yes",
                   "Yes",
                   "Coaching, Notes, Textbook, Group Study, Mixed"),
  Interpretation = c("Coefficients show Private vs Public difference",
                     "Coefficients show improvement over No Formal Education",
                     "Coefficients show improvement over Poor sleep",
                     "Coefficients show effect of longer commute vs shortest",
                     "Coefficient shows effect of participation",
                     "Coefficient shows effect of having internet",
                     "Coefficients show difference from Online Videos")
)

reference_table |>
  kable(col.names = c("Variable", "Reference Category", "Other Levels", "Interpretation")) |>
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"), font_size = 11)
```

## Coefficient Table with Confidence Intervals

```{r}
#| label: tbl-coefficients-full
#| tbl-cap: "Final model coefficients with standard errors and 95% confidence intervals"

# Extract model parameters
params <- model_parameters(final_model, ci = 0.95, ci_method = "residual")

# Create formatted table
params |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  mutate(
    Significance = case_when(
      p < 0.001 ~ "***",
      p < 0.01 ~ "**",
      p < 0.05 ~ "*",
      p < 0.10 ~ ".",
      TRUE ~ ""
    ),
    CI = paste0("[", round(CI_low, 2), ", ", round(CI_high, 2), "]")
  ) |>
  select(Parameter, Coefficient, SE, CI, t, p, Significance) |>
  kable(digits = c(0, 3, 3, 0, 2, 4, 0),
        col.names = c("Term", "Estimate (β)", "Std. Error", "95% CI", "t-value", "p-value", ""),
        align = "lrrrrrr") |>
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"), font_size = 10) |>
  footnote(general = "Signif. codes: *** p<0.001, ** p<0.01, * p<0.05, . p<0.10",
           general_title = "")
```

## Interpretation of Key Effects

We interpret the six most important coefficients, focusing on practical significance (effect magnitude in meaningful units) rather than relying solely on p-values.

### 1. Attendance Rate (`attend_pct`)

```{r}
#| echo: false
attend_coef <- coef(final_model)["attend_pct"]
attend_ci <- confint(final_model)["attend_pct", ]
```

**Estimate**: $\hat{\beta} = `r round(attend_coef, 3)`$ points per percentage point (95% CI: [`r round(attend_ci[1], 3)`, `r round(attend_ci[2], 3)`])

**Interpretation**: Each additional percentage point of class attendance is associated with approximately **0.45 points** higher exam score, holding all other variables constant.

**Practical significance**: Consider a meaningful increment of 20 percentage points (e.g., improving from 70% to 90% attendance):
$$\Delta \hat{y} = 0.454 \times 20 = 9.1 \text{ points}$$
This is both statistically significant ($p < 0.001$) and practically meaningful.

### 2. Study Hours (`study_hrs`) — Conditional on Sleep Quality

Due to the interaction term, the effect of study hours depends on sleep quality. The main effect coefficient represents the slope **for students with Poor sleep quality** (the reference category).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-study-effect
#| tbl-cap: "Marginal effect of one additional hour of study, by sleep quality"

# Extract coefficients
beta_study <- coef(final_model)["study_hrs"]
beta_int_avg <- coef(final_model)["study_hrs:sleep_qualAverage"]
beta_int_good <- coef(final_model)["study_hrs:sleep_qualGood"]

# Calculate total effects
effect_poor <- beta_study
effect_avg <- beta_study + beta_int_avg
effect_good <- beta_study + beta_int_good

# Create table
study_effects <- data.frame(
  Sleep_Quality = c("Poor (reference)", "Average", "Good"),
  Main_Effect = c(round(beta_study, 3), round(beta_study, 3), round(beta_study, 3)),
  Interaction = c("—", round(beta_int_avg, 3), round(beta_int_good, 3)),
  Total_Effect = c(round(effect_poor, 3), round(effect_avg, 3), round(effect_good, 3)),
  Interpretation = c(
    paste0("Each +1h → +", round(effect_poor, 2), " points"),
    paste0("Each +1h → +", round(effect_avg, 2), " points"),
    paste0("Each +1h → +", round(effect_good, 2), " points")
  )
)

study_effects |>
  kable(col.names = c("Sleep Quality", "Main Effect (β₂)", "Interaction (λ)", 
                      "Total Effect", "Interpretation"),
        align = "lccrl") |>
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"))
```

**Key insight**: The benefit of studying is nearly **three times greater** for well-rested students (3.05 points/hour) compared to sleep-deprived students (1.16 points/hour). This interaction is highly significant and has important practical implications: **optimizing sleep may be as important as optimizing study time**.

### 3. Commute Time (`trav_time`)

```{r}
#| echo: false
trav_coefs <- coef(final_model)[grep("trav_time", names(coef(final_model)))]
```

**Estimates** (relative to <15 Min):
- 15-30 Min: $\hat{\beta} = -0.13$ points (not significant, $p = 0.73$)
- 30-60 Min: $\hat{\beta} = -1.77$ points ($p < 0.001$)
- \>60 Min: $\hat{\beta} = -3.75$ points ($p < 0.001$)

**Interpretation**: Students with long commutes (>60 minutes) score approximately **3.75 points lower** than students with short commutes (<15 minutes), holding all else constant. The effect shows that longer commutes are associated with lower scores.

**Practical significance**: The 3.75-point penalty for very long commutes is meaningful but smaller than the effects of attendance and study habits.

### 4. School Type (`school_type`)

**Estimate**: Private vs Public: $\hat{\beta} = 2.13$ points (95% CI: [1.57, 2.68], $p < 0.001$)

**Interpretation**: Students in private schools score **2.1 points higher** than students in public schools.

**Discussion**: This is statistically significant. The true school type effect may reflect unmeasured factors (teacher quality, peer effects, resources) not captured by our predictors.

### 5. Parental Education (`parent_educ`)

```{r}
#| echo: false
parent_coefs <- coef(final_model)[grep("parent_educ", names(coef(final_model)))]
```

**Estimates** (relative to No Formal Education):
- High School: +0.72 points (not significant)
- Graduate: +1.32 points ($p = 0.005$)
- Post Grad 1: +1.80 points ($p < 0.001$)
- Post Grad 2: +2.44 points ($p < 0.001$)
- PhD: +1.89 points ($p < 0.001$)

**Interpretation**: Students with more educated parents tend to score higher. The maximum difference is approximately **2.4 points** between students whose parents have Post Graduate education and those with no formal parental education.

**Note**: The non-monotonic pattern (Post Grad 2 > PhD) may reflect sampling variation or different distributions of other characteristics across these groups.

### 6. Sleep Duration (`sleep_hrs`)

**Estimate**: $\hat{\beta} = 2.27$ points per hour (95% CI: [1.91, 2.63], $p < 0.001$)

**Interpretation**: Each additional hour of sleep is associated with **2.27 points** higher exam score.

**Practical significance**: A student who increases sleep from 6 to 8 hours (a 2-hour increase) would be expected to score approximately **4.5 points higher**. This reinforces the importance of adequate rest for academic performance.

## Interaction Effect Visualization

```{r}
#| label: fig-interaction
#| fig-cap: "Predicted exam scores by study hours and sleep quality. Lines show model predictions holding other variables at reference levels (Public school, No Formal parent education, <15 Min commute, No extracurricular activities, No internet, Online Videos study method) and median values for continuous predictors. Steeper slopes indicate greater benefit from additional study time."
#| fig-height: 5

# Create prediction grid
study_vals <- seq(2, 14, by = 0.5)  # Realistic range of study hours
sleep_levels <- levels(data_train$sleep_qual)

# Build prediction data frame
grid_interact <- expand.grid(
  study_hrs = study_vals,
  sleep_qual = factor(sleep_levels, levels = sleep_levels)
) |>
  mutate(
    attend_pct = median(data_train$attend_pct),
    sleep_hrs = median(data_train$sleep_hrs),
    school_type = factor("Public", levels = levels(data_train$school_type)),
    parent_educ = factor("No Formal", levels = levels(data_train$parent_educ)),
    trav_time = factor("<15 Min", levels = levels(data_train$trav_time)),
    extra_act = factor("No", levels = levels(data_train$extra_act)),
    web_access = factor("No", levels = levels(data_train$web_access)),
    study_method = factor("Online Videos", levels = levels(data_train$study_method))
  )

# Generate predictions
grid_interact$predicted <- predict(final_model, newdata = grid_interact)

# Create plot
ggplot(grid_interact, aes(x = study_hrs, y = predicted, 
                          color = sleep_qual, linetype = sleep_qual)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.3) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c("Poor" = "#E41A1C", "Average" = "#FF7F00", "Good" = "#4DAF4A"),
    name = "Sleep Quality"
  ) +
  scale_linetype_manual(
    values = c("Poor" = "dashed", "Average" = "dotdash", "Good" = "solid"),
    name = "Sleep Quality"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Interaction Effect: Study Hours × Sleep Quality",
    subtitle = "Effect of study time depends on sleep quality — well-rested students benefit more",
    x = "Study Hours per Day",
    y = "Predicted Exam Score"
  ) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom",
        plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "gray40"))
```

**Interpretation of interaction plot**:

1. **All slopes are positive**: Studying more is beneficial regardless of sleep quality
2. **Slopes differ by sleep quality**: The green line (Good sleep) is steepest; the red line (Poor sleep) is flattest
3. **Lines diverge at higher study hours**: At low study hours (2–4), the three groups have similar scores. At high study hours (10–14), well-rested students pull significantly ahead.
4. **Crossover point**: At approximately 6 hours of study, students with Average sleep begin to outperform those with Good sleep who study less — illustrating that high study effort can partially compensate for suboptimal sleep.

## Scenario-Based Predictions

To illustrate the practical implications of our model, we construct two contrasting student profiles and compare their predicted exam scores.

# Create comparison table

- **Profile B** (engaged student): Predicted score of **`r round(pred_B[1, "fit"], 1)`** points (95% CI: [`r round(pred_B[1, "lwr"], 1)`, `r round(pred_B[1, "upr"], 1)`])
- **Difference**: approximately **`r round(pred_B[1, "fit"] - pred_A[1, "fit"], 1)`** points

The confidence intervals do not overlap, indicating that the difference between profiles is statistically significant. The 50-point gap illustrates the substantial variation in outcomes associated with different combinations of behavioral and socioeconomic factors.

<!-- ======================================================================== -->
# Predictive Evaluation {#sec-prediction}
<!-- ======================================================================== -->

## Validation Strategy

To assess the predictive performance of our models and guard against overfitting, we employed a **train/test split** validation strategy:

```{r}
#| label: validation-protocol

cat("=" |> rep(70) |> paste(collapse = ""), "\n")
cat("VALIDATION PROTOCOL\n")
cat("=" |> rep(70) |> paste(collapse = ""), "\n")

cat("\nMethod: Random train/test split\n")
cat("Random seed: set.seed(42) for reproducibility\n")
cat("Split mechanism: Bernoulli(0.70) assignment to training set\n")
cat("\nResulting split:\n")
cat("  Training set: ", nrow(data_train), " observations (", 
    round(100 * nrow(data_train) / nrow(data_clean), 1), "%)\n", sep = "")
cat("  Test set:     ", nrow(data_test), " observations (",
    round(100 * nrow(data_test) / nrow(data_clean), 1), "%)\n", sep = "")
cat("\nNote: All models were fit on training data only.\n")
cat("Test set was used exclusively for final performance evaluation.\n")
```

**Data leakage prevention**: All model fitting, variable selection, and hyperparameter decisions (e.g., which interaction to include) were made using only the training data. The test set was held out and used only for the final performance evaluation reported below.

## Performance Metrics on Test Set

We evaluate three models on the held-out test set:

1. **Null model** (baseline): Predicts the training mean for all observations
2. **Full model** (M3): All predictors, no interaction
3. **Final model** (M4): All predictors + `study_hrs × sleep_qual` interaction

```{r}
#| label: test-performance

# Generate predictions on test set
pred_null <- predict(mod_null, newdata = data_test)
pred_full <- predict(mod3_full, newdata = data_test)
pred_final <- predict(final_model, newdata = data_test)

# Function to calculate metrics
calc_metrics <- function(actual, predicted) {
  residuals <- actual - predicted
  mse <- mean(residuals^2)
  rmse <- sqrt(mse)
  mae <- mean(abs(residuals))
  medae <- median(abs(residuals))
  ss_res <- sum(residuals^2)
  ss_tot <- sum((actual - mean(actual))^2)
  r2 <- 1 - (ss_res / ss_tot)
  return(c(MSE = mse, RMSE = rmse, MAE = mae, MedAE = medae, R2 = r2))
}

# Calculate metrics for each model
m_null <- calc_metrics(data_test$y, pred_null)
m_full <- calc_metrics(data_test$y, pred_full)
m_final <- calc_metrics(data_test$y, pred_final)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-test-performance
#| tbl-cap: "Predictive performance comparison on test set (n = 1,547)"

performance_table <- data.frame(
  Model = c("Null (baseline)", "Full (no interaction)", "Final (with interaction)"),
  MSE = round(c(m_null["MSE"], m_full["MSE"], m_final["MSE"]), 3),
  RMSE = round(c(m_null["RMSE"], m_full["RMSE"], m_final["RMSE"]), 3),
  MAE = round(c(m_null["MAE"], m_full["MAE"], m_final["MAE"]), 3),
  MedAE = round(c(m_null["MedAE"], m_full["MedAE"], m_final["MedAE"]), 3),
  R2 = round(c(m_null["R2"], m_full["R2"], m_final["R2"]), 4)
)

performance_table |>
  kable(col.names = c("Model", "MSE", "RMSE", "MAE", "MedAE", "R²"),
        align = "lrrrrr") |>
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover")) |>
  row_spec(3, bold = TRUE, background = "#e8f5e9")
```

**Interpretation**:

- **MSE (Mean Squared Error)**: The final model achieves MSE = 60.81, substantially lower than the null model (222.38) and slightly better than the full model without interaction (63.90)
- **RMSE (Root MSE)**: The final model has RMSE = 7.80 points — this is the typical prediction error in the original units of the response variable
- **MedAE (Median Absolute Error)**: At 5.16 points, half of all predictions are within 5 points of the true score
- **Out-of-sample R²**: The final model explains 72.61% of variance in the test set, nearly identical to training performance

## Improvement over Baseline

```{r}
#| label: baseline-improvement

cat("=" |> rep(70) |> paste(collapse = ""), "\n")
cat("IMPROVEMENT OVER BASELINE\n")
cat("=" |> rep(70) |> paste(collapse = ""), "\n")

rmse_improvement <- (m_null["RMSE"] - m_final["RMSE"]) / m_null["RMSE"] * 100
mse_improvement <- (m_null["MSE"] - m_final["MSE"]) / m_null["MSE"] * 100
r2_gain <- m_final["R2"] - m_null["R2"]

cat("\nBaseline (Null) RMSE: ", round(m_null["RMSE"], 2), "\n", sep = "")
cat("Final Model RMSE:     ", round(m_final["RMSE"], 2), "\n", sep = "")
cat("RMSE Reduction:       ", round(rmse_improvement, 1), "%\n\n", sep = "")

cat("Baseline (Null) MSE:  ", round(m_null["MSE"], 2), "\n", sep = "")
cat("Final Model MSE:      ", round(m_final["MSE"], 2), "\n", sep = "")
cat("MSE Reduction:        ", round(mse_improvement, 1), "%\n\n", sep = "")

cat("R² gain (vs baseline): ", round(r2_gain, 4), "\n", sep = "")
```

The final model reduces RMSE by **47.7%** compared to the baseline and explains an additional **72.8 percentage points** of variance beyond what predicting the mean achieves.

## Calibration Check

A well-calibrated model produces predictions that closely track observed values across the entire range of the outcome. We assess calibration by plotting predicted vs. observed scores.

```{r}
#| label: fig-calibration
#| fig-cap: "Calibration plot: Predicted vs Observed exam scores on the test set. Red dashed line shows perfect calibration (y = x). Green line shows the actual relationship (linear fit to predictions). Close alignment indicates good calibration."
#| fig-height: 5

calibration_data <- data.frame(
  Observed = data_test$y,
  Predicted = pred_final
)

ggplot(calibration_data, aes(x = Observed, y = Predicted)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3, color = "steelblue", size = 1.5) +
  geom_abline(intercept = 0, slope = 1, color = "red", 
              linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE, color = "darkgreen", 
              alpha = 0.2, linewidth = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Calibration: Predicted vs Observed",
    subtitle = paste0("Test Set (n = ", nrow(data_test), ") | RMSE = ", 
                      round(m_final["RMSE"], 2), " | R² = ", round(m_final["R2"], 3)),
    x = "Observed Exam Score",
    y = "Predicted Exam Score"
  ) +
  coord_fixed(ratio = 1, xlim = c(10, 100), ylim = c(10, 100)) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 12)
```

**Calibration assessment**: The green fitted line closely follows the red diagonal line of perfect calibration across the entire range of observed scores (approximately 10–100). This indicates that:

1. The model is well-calibrated — predictions are accurate across low, medium, and high performers
2. There is no systematic over- or under-prediction at any range
3. The spread around the diagonal is relatively constant (homoscedasticity holds in prediction)

## Residuals Distribution on Test Set

```{r}
#| label: fig-test-residuals
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of prediction residuals on the test set. Centered near zero with symmetric spread indicates unbiased predictions."
#| fig-height: 4

test_residuals <- data_test$y - pred_final

ggplot(data.frame(residuals = test_residuals), aes(x = residuals)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), bins = 40,
                 fill = "steelblue", color = "white", alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_density(color = "red", linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Test Set Residuals Distribution",
    subtitle = paste0("Mean = ", round(mean(test_residuals), 3),
                      " | Median = ", round(median(test_residuals), 3),
                      " | SD = ", round(sd(test_residuals), 2)),
    x = "Residuals (Observed - Predicted)",
    y = "Density"
  ) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 12)
```

**Assessment**: The residuals are centered at zero (mean = -0.05, median = -0.08) and approximately symmetric. This confirms that predictions are unbiased on the test set.

## Overfitting Assessment

```{r}
#| label: tbl-overfitting
#| tbl-cap: "Comparison of model performance on training vs test data"

overfit_check <- data.frame(
  Metric = c("R²", "Adjusted R² / R²", "RMSE"),
  Training = c(
    round(summary(final_model)$r.squared, 4),
    round(summary(final_model)$adj.r.squared, 4),
    round(summary(final_model)$sigma, 3)
  ),
  Test = c(
    round(m_final["R2"], 4),
    round(m_final["R2"], 4),  # Same as R² for test (no adjustment)
    round(m_final["RMSE"], 3)
  ),
  Difference = c(
    round(summary(final_model)$r.squared - m_final["R2"], 4),
    round(summary(final_model)$adj.r.squared - m_final["R2"], 4),
    round(m_final["RMSE"] - summary(final_model)$sigma, 3)
  ),
  Assessment = c("Minimal difference", "Minimal difference", "Test actually lower")
)

overfit_check |>
  kable(col.names = c("Metric", "Training", "Test", "Difference", "Assessment"),
        align = "lrrrr") |>
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"))
```

**Overfitting assessment**: There is **no evidence of overfitting**:

- The R² difference between training (0.7284) and test (0.7261) is only 0.0023
- Remarkably, the test RMSE (7.80) is slightly *lower* than the training RMSE (7.92)
- The consistency between training and test performance indicates that our 24-parameter model does not overfit the $n = 3,453$ training observations

<!-- ======================================================================== -->
# Conclusion {#sec-conclusion}
<!-- ======================================================================== -->

## Summary of Findings

This analysis examined factors associated with academic performance in a sample of 5,000 students using multiple linear regression with interaction effects. Our final model explains approximately **72.6%** of the variance in exam scores (test set R² = 0.726) with an MSE of **60.81** and RMSE of **7.80 points**.

**Key findings**:

1. **Attendance is the strongest predictor**: Each percentage point of attendance is associated with approximately 0.45 additional points on the exam ($\beta = 0.454$, 95% CI: [0.42, 0.48]). A student who improves attendance from 70% to 90% could expect nearly 9 points higher scores, all else equal.

2. **Study hours matter, but sleep quality amplifies the effect**: The benefit of additional study time depends strongly on sleep quality. Well-rested students gain approximately **3.05 points** per additional hour of study, compared to only **1.16 points** for sleep-deprived students — nearly a **3-fold difference** in returns to study effort. This interaction effect is highly significant ($F = 118$, $p < 0.001$).

3. **Commute time has a cumulative negative effect**: Students with commutes exceeding 60 minutes score approximately 3.75 points lower than those with short commutes (<15 min), potentially reflecting both reduced study time and increased fatigue.

4. **School type and parental background matter**: Private school students score about 2.1 points higher than public school students after controlling for other factors. Parental education shows a gradient effect, with higher parental education associated with better student performance (up to +2.4 points for Post Grad vs No Formal).

5. **Age and gender are not predictive**: After controlling for behavioral and socioeconomic factors, neither age nor gender shows any association with exam scores. Residual plots confirm this finding.

## Practical Significance

The most actionable finding concerns the **interaction between study effort and sleep quality**. While educators and parents often emphasize studying more, our results suggest that *how rested* a student is may be equally important. 

- A sleep-deprived student who increases study time from 5 to 10 hours gains only about **5.8 points**
- A well-rested student making the same increase gains about **15.3 points**

For a "struggling student" profile (60% attendance, 2 hours study, poor sleep, long commute, no internet access), our model predicts a score of approximately **30.6 points** (95% CI: [29.1, 32.1]). For an "engaged student" profile (95% attendance, 10 hours study, good sleep, short commute, full resources), the predicted score is approximately **80.1 points** (95% CI: [78.9, 81.2]) — a gap of nearly **50 points**. 

This illustrates both the strong predictive power of the model and the substantial variation in outcomes associated with different student profiles.

## Limitations

Several limitations should be considered when interpreting these results:

1. **Observational data**: This is a cross-sectional observational study. While we can identify strong associations, we cannot establish causality. For example, the association between attendance and scores could reflect reverse causality (students who are doing well are more motivated to attend) or confounding by unmeasured variables (e.g., motivation, family support, prior ability).

2. **Self-reported data**: Variables like study hours and sleep quality may be subject to reporting bias. Students may overestimate study time or misreport sleep patterns.

3. **Generalizability**: The sample may not be representative of all student populations. Results may differ in other educational contexts, cultures, or age groups.

4. **Model assumptions**: Although diagnostic tests suggest the regression assumptions are satisfied, the model is fundamentally linear. True relationships may include nonlinearities or threshold effects not captured by our specification.

5. **Unmeasured confounders**: Important variables such as motivation, prior academic achievement, learning disabilities, or family involvement are not included in the dataset and may confound our estimates.
